newsitem.title: CANADA: End the scandals, Canadian minister tells military.
newsitem.headline: End the scandals, Canadian minister tells military.

text.p: Defence Minister Doug Young on Tuesday called on the Canadian military, reeling from a seemingly endless series of scandals, to bring any remaining skeletons out of the closet.
"We can't sustain it. There is no doubt in my mind this death by a thousand cuts cannot be sustained," Young told a news conference.
"That's why I plead with people that if they have information...let's get it over with. Let's get it out there. Let's wash the linen. Let's clean it up."
The country's second highest officer, Lt. Gen. Armand Roy, was fired on Friday for what the army said were irregularities with his expenses.

A Montreal newspaper reported on Monday that Canada's first female infantry officer, Capt. Sandra Perron, had been beaten and tied to a tree, barefoot in the snow, during a mock capture by enemy forces in 1992.
Young also announced he was freezing all promotion of officers until the end of March, at which time he would report to Prime Minister Jean Chretien on "the future of the Canadian forces."

The Chief of Defence staff, Lt. Gen. Jean Boyle, was forced out as Canada's top soldier in October over an alleged cover-up of the torturing and killing of several Somalis by Canadian peacekeepers in 1993.
That left Vice Chief of Defence Staff, Vice Admiral Larry Murray, filling in for Boyle with Roy as his deputy. Murray is now the only one of Canada's top three officers left.
Boyle's main backer, David Collenette, resigned as defence minister in October.

The public reason was that he broke cabinet guidelines by writing to an immigration official on behalf of a constituent. But commentators and opposition politicians suggested he was forced out because of his handling of the Somalia affair.

For much of 1996, Canadian television viewers were bombarded with daily reports from a public inquiry into the Somali incidents, which also forced the disbanding of the once-proud Canadian Airborne Regiment.
With an eye on elections expected sometime in 1997, Young is eager to be seen to have cleaned up the Canadian armed forces.
He said the incident involving Perron, who has made no complaint to the military, showed a lack of tolerance for women by some soldiers.
"There is no doubt that she was singled out and she was treated more harshly than would normally have been the case, because she was a woman," he said.
